sections.h2: Defaults, not accuracy, drive the case for prepaid smart meters

chart.title: About 9% of conventional postpaid bills default on average, up to 30% in some areas
chart.sub: Share of conventional postpaid PNG bills in default, %.
chart.source: PNGRB committee report, citing CGD entities' submissions.

sections.means: Gas companies gain most from prepaid meters, because they remove the risk of unpaid bills.
sections.todo: Check whether PNGRB's own figures on defaults hold up before accepting the case for prepaid billing.

sections.h2: Smart meters cost far more upfront than a conventional meter

chart.title: Quoted smart-meter prices sit well above a conventional meter's ₹800–1,000
chart.sub: Upfront price per meter, ₹, excluding GST for orders above 1 lakh units.

sections.means: Smart meters carry much higher upfront prices, and the committee would have gas companies pay them.
sections.todo: Watch whether the final cost allocation keeps these meter costs off consumers' bills.

sections.h2: The committee finds no manufacturing bottleneck for the rollout

chart.title: Capacity of about 35 lakh meters a year exceeds about 10 lakh new connections

sections.means: On the committee's own arithmetic, factories can supply new connections without a shortage.
sections.todo: Check whether capacity still holds once the much larger replacement volumes are counted.

sections.h2: Every domestic meter is due to be smart by 1 April 2030

chart.title: Conversion runs in phases, with all meters smart from 1 April 2030
events: Phase IV: remaining connections; all meters smart from 1 April 2030

sections.means: The committee sets a phased schedule for replacing existing meters, ending with smart meters only from 1 April 2030.
sections.todo: Track whether PNGRB notifies the T4S amendment that these deadlines depend on.
